title: Articles and quantifiers
tagline: Choose a, an, the or nothing at all, then say exactly how much or how many with the right word.
why: Small words like a, the and enough are exactly what the open cloze tests, because they're easy to leave out and hard to hear in fast speech. Knowing go to school (no article) from go to the school (a specific building), and few from a few, makes your writing sound careful rather than translated.

hook.text: Nadia checks the camping list: "We need a tent, the big one from Liam's garage, and enough water for everyone." Mateo: "I've packed too much food and too few torches!" Sofia: "Typical. Every trip, the same problem."
hook.ask: Look at a, the, enough, too much, too few and every. Which words point to one specific thing everyone already knows about, and which ones tell you how much or how many?

head: Quantifier
Use with
Example
rows: We don't have enough chairs, but plenty of food.
a few / few, a little / little
I have a few friends here; she has little money left.

use.point: a/an, the, or nothing at all

examples.text: Mateo bought a new sleeping bag for the trip.
examples.note: a = one of many, first time we hear about it
the = the specific one we already know about

examples.text: We always have breakfast before we leave.
Nadia goes to school by bus, but on Saturdays she walks to the school for football practice.
examples.note: school (general purpose) vs the school (the building)

use.point: too much / too many, enough, plenty of

examples.text: We packed too many bags for one car.
There's too much food for four people.
Have we got enough water for the whole weekend?
examples.note: enough = just the right amount, or the minimum needed

examples.text: Don't worry, there's plenty of time before it gets dark.

use.point: a few / few, a little / little

examples.text: I brought a few torches, so we're fine.
examples.note: a few = some, a positive idea

examples.text: We have few torches left — we need to buy more.
examples.note: few = almost none, a negative idea

examples.text: There's a little water in this bottle still.
There's little water left — we should find more soon.
Most of the campers arrived on time.
Neither of the tents is big enough.
examples.note: neither = not one, not the other (two things)

watch_out.wrong: I go to the school every day.
watch_out.why: No article when you mean school for its usual purpose — studying.

watch_out.wrong: He plays the football on Saturdays.
watch_out.why: No article with sports and games.

watch_out.wrong: There is too much bags in the car.
watch_out.right: There are too many bags in the car.
watch_out.why: many + countable plural, much + uncountable — and the verb must agree too (are).

watch_out.wrong: We have a little friends here.
watch_out.why: a few is for countable nouns (friends); a little is for uncountable nouns.
Neither of + plural noun, even though the verb stays singular (works).
each and every always take a singular noun, never a plural one.

l1.es: Voy a la escuela todos los días.
l1.wrong: I go to the school every day.
l1.why: Spanish always uses the article with places like school; English drops it when you mean the usual activity there.

l1.wrong: I play the football on Saturdays.
l1.why: Spanish al keeps the article; English never uses one with sports.
Spanish poco/poca doesn't show countable/uncountable, but English needs few for friends and little for uncountable nouns.
Spanish uses the article with abstract or general ideas, but English talks about them with no article at all.

remember.trick: A = one of many. THE = the one we both know!
remember.tip: Ask yourself: could my listener point to exactly this one? Yes → the. No, just any one → a/an.

dialogue.title: Packing for the camping trip
dialogue.context: Nadia, Mateo, Sofia and Liam are packing the car before a camping weekend in the mountains near Lima and checking they have everything they need.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: We need a tent — the big one from Liam's garage.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: It's already in the car. Have we got enough water for everyone?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I think so, but I've packed too much food and too few torches!

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Typical, Mateo. Every trip, the same problem.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Don't worry, there's plenty of time to buy more torches before we leave.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Neither of my torches has batteries, actually.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Most of my things are ready. I just need a few more snacks.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: We already have too many snacks! We need a little more water instead.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: OK, each of us checks one bag before we go.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Good idea. Let's go to the school first to pick up the sleeping bags from the storeroom.

items.sentence: I go to ___ every day to study.
Where's ___ tent we bought last week?
There's ___ noise outside — I can't sleep.
Have we got ___ chairs for everyone?
I have ___ friends in this town — I just moved here.
items.why: few = almost none, a negative idea

items.sentence: There's ___ milk left — enough for one more coffee.
items.why: a little = some, a positive idea

items.sentence: ___ of the tents is big enough for four people.
items.why: neither = not one, not the other (two things)

items.sentence: ___ of the students has to bring water.
items.why: each, not every, can be followed by of + plural noun

practice.instructions: Complete with a, the, or a suitable quantifier.

practice.instructions: Put the words in order. Tap them one by one.

items.answer: We need a tent for the weekend.
Where's the tent we borrowed from Liam?
We packed too many bags for one car.
There's enough water for the whole weekend.
Neither of the torches has batteries.
Each camper has to bring a sleeping bag.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first, using the word given. Use no more than three words.

items.first: This is not just any tent — it's the tent we bought last week.
We don't have the right number of chairs — we need more.
We packed more bags than we needed.
I only know one or two people in this town.
Not one of my two torches works.
All the campers, one by one, must bring their own water bottle.
items.second_end: camper must bring their own water bottle.

can_do: I can choose a/an, the or no article for places, meals and general ideas.
I can use too much/too many, enough and plenty of correctly.
I can use a few/few, a little/little, both/either/neither and each/every correctly.
summary: a/an = one of many, first mention; the = something specific both speakers know.
No article with meals, sports, languages, general plurals, and places used for their usual purpose (school, bed, home).
too much/little go with uncountable nouns; too many/few go with countable nouns.
a few and a little are positive (some); few and little without a are negative (almost none).
both/either/neither talk about two things; each/every always take a singular noun.
